references.text: Moses asks for permission to offer sacrifices to the Lord in the wilderness, reflecting the requirement to give offerings to the Lord your God.
Moses and Aaron ask Pharaoh to let the people go to offer sacrifices to the Lord, the same theme as in Exodus 10:25.
Pharaoh offers compromises regarding the sacrifices, but Moses insists that they must have animals to offer to the Lord.
The continuation of the conversation where Moses explains that they need livestock for burnt offerings and peace offerings to the Lord.
Pharaoh finally grants permission to go and serve the Lord with sheep and cattle, fulfilling Moses' request.
Burnt offering (עֹלָה) is mentioned as an important type of sacrifice to the Lord, using the same terminology found in Exodus 10:25.
Christ declares that God did not desire burnt offerings and sin offerings, but a body was prepared for him – a fulfillment of the sacrificial system.
Direct narrative connection where verse 9 establishes the purpose (to serve God) and verse 25 specifies the religious action.
Theological contrast where Pharaoh uses the demand for sacrifices as mockery, while Moses uses it as a basis for freedom.
Theological contrast: Moses demands the right to offer sacrifices to God, while Jeremiah condemns offerings that have been misused or stripped of their meaning.
Direct narrative connection where 9:13 sets the goal (to serve God) and 10:25 specifies the means (to sacrifice).
